articles.title: Cortical bone geometry and static gravitational loads in neosauropod dinosaurs: Implications for biomechanical constraints on terrestrial gigantism.
articles.authors: Tito Aureliano, Aline M Ghilardi, Holly N Woodward et al.
articles.abstract: Sauropod dinosaurs achieved unprecedented terrestrial gigantism, raising questions about the biomechanical limits of bone under extreme gravitational loads. We estimated static gravitational pressures (Pg) on appendicular cortical bone in neosauropods, including diplodocoids, brachiosaurids, and titanosaurs. We did this by measuring cortical thickness, estimating body masses, and calculating pressures on limb bones. We compared the results with the theoretical fracture thresholds of composite cortical bone (~150-200 MPa) and pure crystalline hydroxyapatite (~1000 MPa). In the largest specimens, Pg remained two orders of magnitude below the compressive strength of hydroxyapatite. These estimates are a conservative lower bound because they assume simultaneous four-limb support. They are also substantially lower (>15 MPa) than the functional failure threshold of composite cortical bone. Dynamic behaviors raise these values: during slow locomotion, a single hindlimb may briefly support the entire hindquarter load, and the weight distribution between fore- and hindlimbs varies markedly with center-of-mass position. Even so, rearing on the hindlimbs in the largest titanosaurs (>25 metric tons) would remain within safe limits defined by composite-bone failure thresholds. Neosauropod lineages show distinct biomechanical strategies. Diplodocoids kept a posteriorly positioned center of mass compatible with facultative bipedal rearing. Brachiosaurids shifted it cranially through neck and forelimb hypertrophy. Titanosaurs reached extreme sizes through enhanced secondary bone remodeling and extensive postcranial pneumatization. Cortical thickening is consistently associated with increasing gravitational loads across Neosauropoda. However, this static model does not test whether it was the primary evolutionary response, compared with other strategies such as trabecular densification and postcranial pneumaticity.

articles.title: Decoupled and diverse: A morphological examination of the two-jaw system in Mormyridae (Osteoglossiformes).
articles.authors: Kassandra L Ford, Rose Peterson, L Patricia Hernandez
articles.abstract: The tongue-bite apparatus (TBA) is a secondary jaw system found in Osteoglossomorpha and, convergently, Salmonidae. It is thought to have similar prey-processing functions as the pharyngeal jaws, possibly allowing the oral jaws to evolve separately for more efficient prey capture. The TBA is incredibly morphologically diverse, but this diversity has not been well documented across Mormyridae, the most speciose family within Osteoglossomorpha. In this study, we examined shape diversity, levels of evolutionary integration and modularity, and rates of evolution of both the TBA and other associated components of the skull in Mormyridae, both across the family and in its two subfamilies, Petrocephalinae and Mormyrinae. Petrocephalinae, the sister group to the rest of Mormyrinae, is less species rich and has evolved independently from Mormyrinae for approximately 50 million years. This has resulted in disparity across the two groups, not only morphologically but also in terms of electric organ discharges. Results of this study support different models of modularity of the skull for these two subfamilies, with Petrocephalines having two modules as compared to Mormyrine's four modules. In both groups, the TBA makes up its own module, often evolving faster than other components of the skull. We propose that this is an example of a truly decoupled two-jaw system, making it unique compared to the pharyngeal and oral jaws of other well-studied groups, such as cichlids and labrids.

articles.title: 3D development of the mouse pelvic girdle: Insights into the musculoskeletal system and vasculature.
articles.authors: Serena C Fernandopulle, Mark A Wright, Nina St Hillaire et al.
articles.abstract: The mouse (Mus musculus) pelvis features an elongated ilium and triangular pubis and ischium characteristic of a small quadruped, whereas humans possess a short, broad, bowl-shaped pelvis specialized for bipedal locomotion and childbirth. Mice are widely used to model osteoporosis, hip dysplasia, and other pelvic pathologies, yet in utero mouse pelvic development has been incompletely characterized, limiting cross-species interpretation. Here, we integrate 3D micro-CT and histology to generate a comprehensive atlas of mouse pelvic development from embryonic days 12.5-18.5 (E12.5-E18.5), focusing on the ilium, hip joint, and sacroiliac joint. We show that E14.5 is a critical stage, when the hip and sacroiliac joints form. We identify a sequential developmental program in mice in which joint cartilage forms first, followed by muscle-cartilage interaction, and, subsequently, extensive blood vessel growth. In contrast to the transversely oriented, developmentally delayed iliac growth and ossification described in recent studies of the human bipedal pelvis, the mouse ilium follows an earlier, centrally initiated, longitudinal ossification pattern. Overall, our atlas provides an essential quadrupedal reference for interpreting human pelvic development, evolution, and disease models.

articles.title: Bioerosion traces in bones reveal an increase in ethological diversity in the insect exploitation of carcasses in the late Triassic.
articles.authors: Lucca S Cunha, Francesco Battista, Heitor Francischini
articles.abstract: This study presents the first detailed description of bioerosion traces produced by insects in bones from the Santa Cruz Sequence (early Carnian, Santa Maria Supersequence, Brazil). An array of traces is reported, consisting of notches, a tube, trails of grooves attributed to the ichnotaxon Osteocallis mandibulus and ornamented depressions attributed to a new ichnotaxon Osteograptus thanatobios igen. nov. et isp. nov. The traces were likely produced by insects, but a less inclusive taxonomic attribution is currently not possible. The ethological interpretation for the bioerosion structures is that they represent feeding traces. This report increases the contrast between the Middle and Late Triassic bioerosion record, since the latter is significantly more diverse and abundant. Hypotheses related to the onset of the Carnian Humid Episode as well as taphonomic biases are discussed as possible explanations for this contrast.

articles.title: Morphological plasticity in the dentition of the lungfish Gnathorhiza from the Permian of Brazil: A population-level geometric morphometric analysis.
articles.authors: Mauro B S Lacerda, Gustavo H N Petreca, Gabriel E B de Barros et al.
articles.abstract: Dental plates are pivotal in the lungfish paleontological record, constituting highly mineralized structures resilient to diagenetic processes. This study provides a detailed description and quantitative shape analysis of 95 newly discovered Gnathorhiza sp. dental plates from the Middle-Late Permian Corumbataí Formation, Brazil. The analyzed sample comprises both upper and lower dentition morphotypes, sharing diagnostic generic features such as straight, sharp, and narrow conical ridges, an obtuse angle between the first and last ridges, a slightly conical lingual border, deep sulci, and an occlusal surface displaying reticulated ornamentation with distinct petrodentine cores. Taphonomic systematization suggests distinct preservation histories for each morphotype, explaining the overrepresentation of upper plates relative to lower ones. To quantitatively evaluate structural variation, landmark-based geometric morphometrics was applied to both upper and lower tooth plates; however, due to a significantly larger sample size, the upper dentition yielded the most robust and biologically significant results. The geometric morphometric analyses revealed substantial morphological variance, particularly localized in the first ridge and first sulcus of the upper plates. Rather than resulting from strict ontogenetic developmental paths or sexual dimorphism, we hypothesize that these predominant morphological differences reflect high phenotypic plasticity within this isolated population. This study confirms the high abundance of Gnathorhiza in the Corumbataí Formation, provides a rigorous assessment of key morphological features in late Paleozoic dipnoan dental plates, and offers insights into the population dynamics of these specialized durophagous predators within a complex Permian mega-lake paleoenvironment.

articles.title: Axial Complex of Deep-Sea Acorn Worm Quatuoralisia malakhovi (Hemichordata, Enteropneusta, Torquaratoridae).
articles.authors: Olga V Ezhova, Anastasiya I Lukinykh, Vladimir V Malakhov
articles.abstract: The axial complex (proboscis complex or heart-kidney) is well-studied for the shallow-living enteropneusts that burrow into the sediment and use the muscular proboscis as the primary locomotor organ. However, the deep-sea enteropneusts in the family Torquaratoridae are epibenthic surface-dwellers with a dispersed, poorly developed proboscis musculature. There is little data on the structure of their axial complex (AC). We have studied in detail the microscopic anatomy of the AC of three specimens of torquaratorid Quatuoralisia malakhovi Ezhova et Lukinykh, 2022. The proboscis of Q. malakhovi is widely fused with the collar along the entire dorsal side rather than being connected by a narrow stalk. The AC includes the buccal diverticulum (stomochord), pericardium, glomerulus (axial organ) and associated blood vessels, perihaemal coeloms, and proboscis skeletal elements. The latter are two separate symmetrical plates supporting the buccal diverticulum laterally. The buccal diverticulum is elongated in transverse direction and packed with large, vacuolated cells without a lumen. It is completely separated from the main course of the gut. The pericardium lies on the dorsal side of the buccal diverticulum. The heart is absent. The glomerulus consists of two symmetrical extensions separated by the confluence of the dorsal blood vessel. The latter is accompanied by the perihaemal coeloms and splits into several branches resembling the mouth of a river, which then flow into the glomerulus. Two buccal blood vessels with folded walls run from the sides of the glomerulus to the ventral blood vessel. A protocoelomic coelomopore is absent, however we found a pair of mesocoelomic coelomoducts and coelomopores. The torquaratorid AC demonstrates varying degrees of reduction. None of the previously studied species of Torquaratoridae possesses a complete set of AC components characteristic of shallow-living enteropneusts. Torquaratoridae are derived in terms of structure and composition of the AC compared to non-torquaratorid hemichordates.

articles.title: Biological Insights From the Osteohistology of a Nile Crocodile.
articles.authors: Ayanda Buso, Maria Eugenia Pereyra, Anusuya Chinsamy
articles.abstract: While long bones are mostly utlised for skeletochronology of extant and extinct vertebrates, among crocodilians, dermal bones have also been studied. However, there is a lack of a systematic and comprehensive study of the variation in osteohistology and skeletochronology of limb, axial, and dermal bones of extant crocodilians. Here, we undertake a comprehensive assessment of the histology of multiple postcranial elements of a single, captive adult Crocodylus niloticus (with approximately known age) to assess their utility for skeletochronology. We document the intraskeletal histological variability in the skeleton and show that despite the gastralia recording the highest number of growth rings, the radius, ulna, and fibula are more reliable for skeletochronology. We show substantial variation in the histology of the osteoderms depending on the plane of sectioning, as well as their location on the body of the crocodile. Additionally, we report that anteriorly sectioned dorsal osteoderms preserved the highest number of growth marks. Our study provides important information regarding intraskeletal variation in osteohistology and presents key information regarding the choice of skeletal elements for reliable life history reconstruction of C. niloticus.

articles.title: Functional Adaptations for Load-Bearing in a Dermal Bone: The Pectoral Fin Spine of the Russian Sturgeon (Huso Gueldenstaedtii).
articles.authors: Esteban Marroquín-Arroyave, Joshua Milgram
articles.abstract: Dermal bone, which forms a variety of skeletal structures and persists in a wide range of extant vertebrates, evolved prior to endochondral bone which forms all mammalian load-bearing long bones. Sturgeons (Acipenseriformes) are an early-diverging extant lineage of actinopterygians that retain prominent post-cranial dermal skeletal elements. They retain a long robust spine at the leading edge of the pectoral fin, called the pectoral fin spines (PFS). PFS are bone elements that are present in many extinct and extant species of non-tetrapod jawed fish. In this study, we characterize the structure (light, polarized, micro-computed tomography and scanning electron microscopy), composition (FTIR, TGA, BMD), and mechanical properties (3-point bending and microindentation) of the PFS of the Russian sturgeon (Huso gueldenstaedtii). The microstructure of the PFS is highly organized as it is formed by dermal osteonal bone and parallel fibered bone. Its microarchitecture, along with high material toughness, anisotropy, and substantial ash content, enables the PFS to bear loads and function in both locomotion and protection. In addition, we show an interconnected network of neurovascular canals and ornamentations, features also found in PFS of other non-tetrapod jawed fish. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that dermal bone can form structurally organized, mechanically competent load-bearing elements and provide new insights into PFSs in ray-finned fish.

articles.title: General Morphology and Neurite Projection Patterns of Supramedullary Neurons in the Cunner, Tautogolabrus adspersus.
articles.authors: Nick Hiza, Jun Liu, Tina Wong et al.
articles.abstract: Supramedullary neurons (SMNs) are located on the dorsal surface of the hindbrain and spinal cord in many adults of teleost fishes. Comparative morphological studies have revealed differences in SMN size, number and distribution among fishes. However, little information exists on the projection patterns of SMN neurites within the central nervous system. We focus on a single species of adult teleost fish, the cunner, Tautogolabrus adspersus, a fish that has 25-46 SMN somata aligned dorsally along the midline in the hindbrain and rostral third of the spinal cord. Light and transmission electron microscopic techniques provide new information on the general morphology of SMNs and Lucifer yellow filled SMNs reveal that these neurons are not morphologically homogeneous. Rather, four different morphotypes can be identified based on projection patterns of major neurites in the hindbrain and spinal cord wholemounts. The morphological variations suggest that some SMNs exit the brain exclusively through the first dorsal root while others exit the central nervous system through a dorsal root and the trigeminal nerve. Despite the remarkable size and accessibility of SMNs, their function(s) remains unknown. One proposed role of these cells is eliciting mucous secretion in response to skin abrasion from predation. Variation in projection patterns in the cunner provides a morphological framework from which to design electrophysiological studies to help reveal SMN function.

articles.title: The Evolutionary History of Early Ray-Finned Fishes (Pan-Actinopterygii).
articles.authors: Jack Stack
articles.abstract: One out of every two vertebrate species is a ray-finned fish (Actinopterygii). The ~380-million-year fossil record of ray-finned fishes provides a window into the evolutionary history of actinopterygian diversity in deep time. The actinopterygian fossil record shows that the ray-finned fish crown group (Actinopterygii) lived alongside speciose members of now extinct lineages, collectively referred to as early actinopterygians. I review the evolutionary history of early actinopterygians through deep time, including morphology, taxonomy, phylogeny, and the fossil record itself, to form a foundation for future research. Early actinopterygians are a paraphyletic assemblage of ~600 extinct species divided between ~22 named clades and the "palaeoniscoids," a taxonomic wastebasket comprised of hundreds of species. Although nearly a decade of phylogenetic research indicates that most early actinopterygians branch off the ray-finned fish stem group, their interrelationships are largely unresolved. Notable gaps in the record of early actinopterygians, which ranges from the Early Devonian to the Early Cretaceous, include a nearly non-existent Early Devonian record, an almost complete lack of Pennsylvanian-Middle Permian marine assemblages, a gap in the Middle Triassic record obscuring the start of a decline in early actinopterygian diversity, and a sparsely documented Jurassic record. We are poised to build a reliable systematic framework for early actinopterygians via novel methods for phylogenetic analysis, fossil imaging, and the increased connectivity of paleoichthyologyists around the globe. The promise of a reliable systematic framework for early actinopterygians is to better describe the entire history of Actinopterygii and actinopterygian macroevolution in deep time.

articles.title: Layered anatomy of the greater and lesser occipital nerves with photogrammetry-based three-dimensional models: a cadaveric study.
articles.authors: Wei Zhou, Haosu Zhang, Lean Sun et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The superficial neurovascular anatomy of the posterior occipital region is important for occipital nerve block, greater occipital nerve (GON) decompression, and posterior fossa incision planning. However, the continuous layered relationship between the medial GON-occipital artery (OA) region and the lateral lesser occipital nerve (LON) channel remains incompletely characterized. METHODS: This cadaveric study examined 10 formalin-fixed specimens (20 sides). Layer-by-layer dissection documented nerve courses, emergence points, diameters, terminal branches, neurovascular relationships, GON-LON communications, and relationships with the OA and adjacent muscles. Photogrammetry-based three-dimensional models were constructed for visualization, not quantitative measurement. RESULTS: The GON and LON were identified on all 20 sides. The GON had 6.0 ± 1.4 terminal branches. Its trapezius muscle/fascial emergence point was located 25.4 ± 3.2 mm horizontally from the posterior midline and 14.0 ± 2.2 mm vertically from the external occipital protuberance (EOP) level. GON-OA relationships comprised a single crossing on 3 sides, multiple crossings on 8 sides, continuous contact on 5 sides, and coiling on 4 sides. The LON traversed a trapezius muscle-related plane on 9 sides and followed a posterior sternocleidomastoid muscle-border course on 11 sides. In descriptive side-level comparisons, the trapezius muscle-related emergence point was closer to the posterior midline and EOP level but farther from the mastoid reference line than the posterior sternocleidomastoid muscle-border emergence point. GON-LON communications were observed on 17 sides. CONCLUSION: These findings support a layered, pathway-based, and conceptual zone-based model of posterior occipital neurovascular anatomy, rather than localization based only on isolated surface landmarks.

articles.title: Facial artery morphology assessed by computed tomography angiography: a mixed-effects morphometric analysis of age, sex, and laterality.
articles.authors: Sindy Melissa Sanchez-Romo, Adrian Manuel Verdines-Perez, Mario Campos-Coy et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The facial artery is the principal arterial supply to the midface and is among the most frequently encountered vascular structures during facial reconstructive, aesthetic, and minimally invasive procedures. Precise knowledge of its anatomical course and morphometric characteristics is essential to minimize vascular complications. However, previous morphometric studies have largely been descriptive and have rarely accounted for bilateral anatomical correlation or simultaneously evaluated the independent effects of age, sex, and laterality using appropriate multivariable statistical models. METHODS: A retrospective cross-sectional study was performed using computed tomography angiography (CTA) examinations from 103 adults, yielding 201 evaluable facial arteries. Standardized three-dimensional morphometric measurements were obtained at the inferior border of the mandible and the lateral alar base. Linear mixed-effects models incorporating patient-specific random intercepts were used to evaluate the effects of age, sex, side, and CTA diagnostic category while accounting for within-subject correlation. Measurement reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman analysis, and Cohen's kappa. RESULTS: Type III, according to the Furukawa classification, was the predominant anatomical pattern (67.2%). Among 98 patients with bilateral visualization, Furukawa type showed complete right-left concordance (100%; κ = 1.00). In an additional patient-level logistic model, neither age (OR 0.992 per year; 95% CI, 0.965-1.020; P = 0.584) nor female sex (OR 1.793; 95% CI, 0.767-4.191; P = 0.178) was significantly associated with Type III versus Type II. For continuous morphometric variables, no systematic laterality effect was detected, although individual-level bilateral agreement varied across parameters. After Holm correction across morphometric outcomes, women had a smaller facial artery diameter at the inferior border of the mandible and a shorter zygomatic arch-facial artery distance than men, while increasing age was independently associated with a shorter oral commissure-facial artery distance. Quantitative morphometric measurements demonstrated good-to-excellent observer reproducibility (intraobserver ICC: 0.900-0.960; interobserver ICC: 0.760-0.860), whereas categorical assessment of facial artery position relative to the nasolabial sulcus showed perfect intraobserver (κ = 1.00) and substantial interobserver agreement (κ = 0.79). CONCLUSIONS: CTA provides a reproducible morphometric assessment of the facial artery. No systematic laterality effect was identified for continuous morphometric variables, although individual bilateral agreement varied by measurement, while Furukawa type showed complete bilateral concordance in patients with both arteries visualized. Age and sex were not significantly associated with Furukawa Type III versus Type II, but they influenced selected continuous morphometric parameters. These findings characterize facial artery anatomy in a Mexican clinical cohort and may inform individualized anatomical assessment and preprocedural planning; they do not establish procedural risk thresholds.

articles.title: The paracondylar process: anatomical relationships and clinical implications.
articles.authors: Beitris Chiu, Nigel Williams, Hong Kuan Kok et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The paracondylar process (PCP) is a rare and infrequently reported anatomical variant, where the incomplete separation of the lowest occipital sclerotome (proatlas) and uppermost cervical sclerotome results in a complete bony projection that meets with an epitransverse process of the atlas. We report a case that highlights the imaging and anatomical relationships of the PCP, particularly with the vertebral artery (VA), which has been given little attention in literature despite its important symptomatic and neurosurgical implications. CASE PRESENTATION: A 55-year-old male presented with longstanding limitation to neck movement, left‑sided headaches and occasional dizzy spells. Cervical computed tomography (CT) imaging demonstrated a bony strut projecting inferiorly from the skull base, laterally adjacent to the left occipital condyle, articulating with the epitransverse process of C1. Though CT angiography was not performed, close examination of the course of the left vertebral artery on the soft tissue CT windows demonstrated an intimate relationship of the artery coursing immediately medial to the bony process in its V3 segment. We present a three-dimensional reconstruction prepared via segmentation and close reading of the soft tissue CT to illuminate the expected course of the vertebral artery and its' relationship to the PCP. CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates the anatomical and clinical significance of the paracondylar process (PCP), with a particular focus on its relationship with the vertebral artery. Whilst rare, this finding carries important clinical implications if surgical resection is to be contemplated.

articles.title: Complex cervical venous drainage with a common facial-paralaryngeal anastomosis receiving the superior thyroid vein.
articles.authors: Mugurel Constantin Rusu, Adelina Maria Jianu, Laura Octavia Grigoriţă et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Tributaries of the internal jugular vein (IJV) may form common trunks or interconnected drainage pathways. We report a complex right-sided cervical venous configuration involving separate facial and lingual-parapharyngeal-paralaryngeal pathways connected by an anastomotic arch receiving the superior thyroid vein. METHODS: An archived computed tomography angiogram (CTA) of a 68-year-old woman was retrospectively reviewed using Horos. Axial source images and three-dimensional volume renderings were assessed bilaterally, and linear measurements were obtained using the software's calliper tool. RESULTS: The common facial vein and a lingual-parapharyngeal-paralaryngeal channel terminated separately in the right IJV and were connected by an anastomotic arch. The superior thyroid vein originated from the left half of the thyroid isthmus, ascended in a left paramedian position, crossed rightwards posterior to the right anterior jugular vein, and joined the inferior end of the arch. Associated findings included right external jugular vein fenestration (2.23 × 0.58 cm) and a posterior external jugular vein connected to the transverse cervical vein by an anastomotic arch. CONCLUSION: This configuration represents interconnected cervical venous drainage pathways and does not establish duplication of a thyrolinguofacial trunk. Recognition of their tributaries, connections and separate jugular terminations may assist imaging interpretation and surgical planning.

articles.title: Left anterior laryngeal loop of the common carotid artery in a cluster of bilateral cervicothoracic vascular variants: a case report.
articles.authors: Viviana Dincă, Adelina Maria Jianu, Mugurel Constantin Rusu
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: The common carotid artery (CCA) normally ascends in the carotid sheath, posterolateral to the larynx and trachea. Anterior or pretracheal CCA courses are rare and have been described mainly on the right, usually in relation to a high-riding brachiocephalic trunk (BCT) or another arch-level anomaly. We report a CTA case with a common-origin left CCA-BCT trunk, a high-riding BCT and bilateral carotid redundancy, including a left anterior laryngeal CCA loop. METHODS: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the aortic arch and bilateral carotid systems was reviewed using multiplanar reformatting and three-dimensional volume-rendered reconstruction. Vessel loops, branching points and relationships to the hyoid-laryngeal framework, thyroid gland and adjacent skeletal landmarks were recorded. RESULTS: CTA showed a common-origin left CCA-BCT trunk with a high-riding BCT measuring 3.27 cm. The right CCA formed a 1.79 cm lateral loop and bifurcated posterolateral to the hyoid-laryngeal framework; the right external carotid artery (ECA) gave rise to a linguofacial trunk and then formed a retromandibular loop. The left CCA formed a 2.15 cm intramediastinal loop and a 1.75 cm anterior laryngeal loop. The left superior thyroid artery arose directly from the CCA. The left ECA showed independent branching and a retromandibular loop. Tortuosity indices ranged from 33.1% to 92.7%; all segments were tortuous and the right internal carotid artery additionally formed a kink (apex angle 87.3°). CONCLUSION: This case documents a rare left anterior laryngeal CCA loop in association with bilateral carotid and external carotid branching variants. The left-sided anterior loop is the main surgical finding because it brings a major cervical artery close to the anterior laryngeal operative field. Recognition of this pattern is relevant before front-of-neck airway access, thyroid surgery, laryngotracheal surgery and central neck procedures.

articles.title: Duty factor is a more prominent modulator of external vertical loading than step frequency during running: a within-subject experimental study.
articles.authors: Aurélien Patoz, David Perrinjaquet, Johan Garcia et al.
articles.abstract: Peak vertical ground reaction force (Fv,max) and vertical average loading rate (VALR) are commonly used to characterize external vertical loading during running. Although increasing step frequency (SF) is frequently used to modify these measures, the observed effects may partly reflect concurrent changes in duty factor (DF). This study determined the independent effects of manipulating DF and SF on Fv,max and VALR during level treadmill running. Fifteen healthy runners completed a preferred-condition trial and eight randomized 5-min trials at 11 km/h. DF was manipulated by ± 16% and ± 8% while SF was maintained at its preferred value, and SF was manipulated by ± 12% and ± 6% while DF was controlled. Preferred DF was strongly and inversely associated with Fv,max (R2 = 0.81, p < 0.001) but not with VALR (R2 = 0.21, p = 0.09). Preferred SF was not associated with either loading measure (p ≥ 0.70). DF manipulation affected Fv,max and VALR (both p ≤ 0.001), whereas SF manipulation affected Fv,max (p < 0.001), driven by the - 12% condition, but not VALR (p = 0.11). Normalized within-participant slopes were more negative for DF than SF for Fv,max (-1.03 ± 0.20 vs 0.07 ± 0.20% per 1% relative change; p < 0.001) and VALR (-0.97 ± 0.94 vs 0.32 ± 1.11%; p = 0.02). During level treadmill running at the submaximal speed investigated, DF produced more consistent and quantitatively larger changes in external vertical loading than SF when the other temporal variable was controlled. These findings identify DF as a more prominent temporal determinant of external vertical loading than SF under the conditions investigated and demonstrate, at both the between- and within-subject levels, the importance of DF in modulating vertical loading.

articles.title: An anatomically based functional upper cervical spinal unit tested under low quasi-static loading for use in an omnidirectional surrogate neck.
articles.authors: Sarah Romani, Paris Vakiel, Peter A Cripton
articles.abstract: Safety devices designed to prevent spinal cord and traumatic brain injuries are often evaluated using anthropometric test devices (ATDs). However, commonly used ATD necks lack biomechanical fidelity under multiplane loading, particularly during low-speed head impacts and axial loading. This study aimed to develop an anatomically-accurate upper cervical spine (UCS) surrogate that exhibits biofidelic kinematic responses under quasi-static flexion-extension, lateral bending, and axial torsion-a preliminary step toward a full neck surrogate capable of simulating complex multiplane loading. CT scans of a healthy 31-year-old male were used to generate vertebral geometry. Based on similarity to cadaveric ligament properties, woven cotton was selected as a ligament surrogate material. Anatomical landmarks were used to define ligament attachment points, and an adjustable attachment system enabled in-situ tensioning. The resulting UCS model was evaluated against post-mortem human subject data under quasi-static loading, assessing neutral zone (NZ), range of motion (ROM), repeatability, and helical axis of motion (HAM) using the CORA method. ROM and NZ values across all joints and degrees of freedom were within one standard deviation of literature values. The model demonstrated excellent repeatability (CORA:0.87-0.97), good biofidelity in flexion-extension (CORA:0.69-0.75; C0-C1 unloading:0.47), good-to-excellent in lateral bending (CORA:0.75-0.94), and fair-to-good in axial rotation (CORA:0.44-0.65). The mean HAM location aligned with cadaveric data in axial rotation and was slightly anterior during flexion-extension. Overall, the UCS model exhibited strong repeatability and biofidelity, supporting its potential as a preliminary component of a full cervical spine surrogate for future multiplane biomechanical research.

articles.title: Transfemoral bone-anchored limbs alter joint-load-line offset during walking.
articles.authors: Brecca M M Gaffney, Dan W Milius, Danielle H Melton et al.
articles.abstract: Individuals with transfemoral amputation are at a heightened risk of musculoskeletal overuse injuries and reduced stability, largely due to altered joint biomechanics. The position of the ground reaction force (GRF) relative to hip and knee joints directly influences both joint biomechanics and dynamic stability and is influenced both by both movement patterns and prosthetic alignment. However, it is unknown if it is influenced by prosthetic suspension type. Our objective was to determine how the position of the GRF relative to hip and knee joint centers during walking differs between individuals with transfemoral amputation using either a socket prosthesis or bone-anchored limb (BAL). Motion capture data was collected from a convenience sample of 17 participants with unilateral transfemoral amputation during overground walking at two timepoints: before and 12-months following BAL implantation. The distances between the GRF line of action and the hip and knee joints in the sagittal and frontal planes were calculated and compared across timepoints (α = 0.05). The distance between the GRF and hip joint center was less medial (p < 0.001) on the amputated limb and more lateral (p < 0.001) on the intact limb during stance period when using a BAL compared to a socket prosthesis. Closer positioning of the GRF relative to the hip joint may reduce frontal plane compensatory strategies required for hip stabilization, potentially reflecting a biomechanical stable gait pattern when using a BAL.

articles.title: Joint-specific kinematic deviations in asymptomatic flatfoot using biplane fluoroscopy.
articles.authors: Andrew C Peterson, Tradd Rector, Elizabeth K Bowman et al.
articles.abstract: Asymptomatic flatfoot (AFF) is characterized by structural features of a medial arch collapse in the absence of pain, yet its dynamic biomechanical characteristics remain understudied. This study aimed to quantify and compare three-dimensional, multi-joint foot and ankle kinematics between individuals with AFF and healthy controls during walking and heel rise tasks using biplane fluoroscopy. Twenty-three participants (13 controls, 10 AFF) underwent weightbearing computed tomography to generate subject-specific bone models. Dynamic in vivo kinematics of the tibia, fibula, talus, and calcaneus were captured using biplane fluoroscopy during walking and heel rise. Joint kinematics for the tibiotalar, subtalar, tibiofibular, and talofibular joints were calculated using model-based tracking and analyzed using statistical parametric mapping. Range of motion (ROM) was also compared between groups. No significant differences in joint kinematics were observed between groups during walking. Walking ROM differences were observed only before FDR correction and were therefore interpreted as exploratory. During heel rise, AFF maintained a more everted subtalar position after SPM FDR correction and demonstrated reduced sagittal plane ROM at the tibiotalar and talofibular joint after ROM FDR correction. These findings indicate that significant group differences were detected during heel rise but not during walking within separate task specific analyses. These task dependent differences provide insight into biomechanical adaptations associated with AFF morphology, although longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these differences are related to future symptom development or deformity progression.

articles.title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
articles.authors: Matthew Slopecki, Edel Fanning, Stacey Kung et al.
articles.abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.

articles.title: Dynamical systems-based metrics reveal fatigue-related biomechanical changes during running in endurance-trained male and female runners.
articles.authors: Yiyang Chen, Jill Emmerzaal, Gleydciane A Fernandes et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Linear and nonlinear metrics derived from a small number of accelerometers provide global insight into fatigue-related changes and injury risk. RESEARCH QUESTION: This study aimed to determine the effects of fatigue on movement dynamics estimated from lower-back accelerometry between endurance-trained male and female runners. METHODS: Thirty-two endurance-trained runners (16 females) performed a fatiguing running task until volitional exhaustion (20 on the Borg CR20 scale), while wearing one inertial measurement unit (IMU) placed on their pelvis/lower back. Step and stride regularity (unbiased autocorrelation), root mean square (RMS)-based measures of variability (absolute RMS and RMS ratio), complexity (Sample Entropy), jerk-based measure of smoothness (Log Dimensionless Jerk; LDLJ), and stability (short- and long-term Lyapunov Exponent) were calculated from the raw accelerations. RESULTS: Significant main effects of fatigue were observed across both sexes for gait regularity, with an 8% reduction in anteroposterior step regularity and an 11% reduction in stride regularity. Fatigue also altered variability characteristics, resulting in a 12% increase in mediolateral absolute RMS, a 13% increase in anteroposterior absolute RMS, a 2% decrease in vertical RMS ratio, a 6% increase in mediolateral RMS ratio, and an 8% increase in anteroposterior RMS ratio. Fatigue increased movement complexity, as evidenced by a 14% increase in vertical Sample Entropy and an 11% increase in anteroposterior Sample Entropy. In addition to these overall fatigue effects, RMS-based measure of variability showed sex-specific responses. Interaction effects showed that males exhibited a 4% increase in the vertical absolute RMS of lower-back acceleration with fatigue, whereas females did not. SIGNIFICANCE: Both male and female endurance-trained runners may adopt a less regular and less predictable whole-body movement pattern with fatigue, while RMS-based variability showed sex-specific responses, with increased fatigue-related changes in males. These findings highlight the importance of considering both general and sex-specific adaptations when monitoring fatigue.

articles.title: Smartphone assessment of postural sway and prospective falls in older adults: A large community-based study.
articles.authors: Patima Silsupadol, Suzanne R O'Brien, Sara Bautista et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Impaired postural control is a key risk factor for falls in older adults. However, laboratory-based postural sway assessments are costly and difficult to implement in real-world environments. Smartphones may offer a portable, low-cost, and easy-to-administer alternative for quantifying postural sway in large-scale community settings. RESEARCH QUESTION: Can a smartphone-embedded accelerometer quantify postural sway, distinguish retrospective fallers from non-fallers, and predict future falls over 12 months? METHODS: A total of 580 adults aged ≥ 55 years were assessed between 2023 and 2026. Fall history was collected, with prospective falls monitored over 12 months. Sway area and path length were measured using the Physiological Profile Assessment swaymeter during four standing conditions (eyes open/closed, firm/foam surfaces). Concurrently, smartphone-derived accelerometer data were used to compute acceleration trajectory area and path length. Pearson correlations, two-way ANOVA, and multivariable logistic regression examined relationships between instruments, group differences, and fall prediction. RESULTS: Smartphone-derived measures were strongly correlated with swaymeter outcomes for area (r = 0.713, p < 0.001) and path length (r = 0.803; p < 0.001). Both systems demonstrated significant group effects for sway area (p < 0.05), and smartphone-derived acceleration trajectory path length differed significantly between fallers and non-fallers (p = 0.036). Adding smartphone-derived acceleration trajectory path length to established risk factors increased Nagelkerke R² from 0.142 to 0.150, but the acceleration measure was not a significant predictor of future falls. SIGNIFICANCE: Smartphone-based accelerometry quantified postural sway and distinguished retrospective fallers from non-fallers but did not improve future fall prediction beyond established risk factors.

articles.title: Effects of cues to walk softly and quietly on gait mechanics during load carriage.
articles.authors: Caleb D Johnson, David J Zeppetelli, Cole A Dempsey et al.
articles.abstract: Walking with load carriage is a routine and necessary activity for many occupations and recreational athletes, however it induces significant physical strain, resulting in high rates of musculoskeletal injury. Gait alteration cues to run softly/quietly have been shown to reduce external forces related to injury in runners. However, the effects of these cues have yet to be explored for load carriage. 38 participants completed testing on an instrumented treadmill while kinematics were tracked via optical motion capture. Participants first completed a habitual load carriage trial (HAB) at a self-selected pace (1.23 ± 0.12 m/s) while carrying an 18 kg weighted vest. They were given a 5-min warm-up followed by data collection. Participants were then cued to modify their gait by walking "quietly and softly" (SOFT), using the same pace as for HAB. Outcome variables were averaged across 20 strides, including peak hip/knee/ankle joint internal sagittal and frontal plane moments, peaks/excursion in joint angles, double-stance time, stride length, and cadence. The SOFT condition resulted in decreased second peak hip abduction and peak knee flexion moments, and second peak vertical forces, but increased peak knee extension moments and first peak vertical forces (p < 0.05, Cohen's d≥0.5). Further, the SOFT condition resulted in increased peak flexion angles (hip/knee) and reduced extension/plantarflexion angles (hip/knee/ankle). Given the conflicting changes in external forces, the results do not support SOFT as a modification to reduce overall musculoskeletal injury risk during load carriage.

articles.title: Transient gait instability during the initial phase of the 6-minute walk test in people with stroke: A nonlinear analysis using inertial measurement units.
articles.authors: Yasuhiro Inui, Yusaku Takamura, Shu Morioka
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In people with stroke (PwS), reduced gait speed and trunk acceleration changes in the latter half of the 6-minute walk test (6MWT) have been reported as fatigue-related, but temporal changes in motor control remain understudied. Clinicians often observe instability immediately after gait onset, yet quantitative evidence is scarce. This study used inertial measurement units (IMUs) and nonlinear analysis to examine fatigue-related changes and post-onset instability during the 6MWT in PwS. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, 19 PwS and 19 age-matched controls completed the 6MWT wearing IMUs at the L5 vertebra and both ankles. Spatiotemporal parameters and stability indices (root mean square, harmonic ratio, sample entropy, short-term Lyapunov exponent [sLE]) were calculated. Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) analyzed the 6-minute period both continuously and by comparing an initial phase (first 60 s) with the subsequent phase. Bayesian and sensitivity analyses were also performed. RESULTS: Continuous-time LMMs showed reduced cadence and increased double-support ratio in PwS. Among stability indices, only mediolateral sLE (sLE-ML) showed a significant group × phase interaction: increasing in the initial phase in PwS but not in controls. Bayesian and sensitivity analyses confirmed this finding was robust and specific to the 60-second cutoff. Initial-phase sLE-ML correlated negatively with Fugl-Meyer lower-extremity scores. CONCLUSIONS: PwS showed fatigue-related gait changes during the 6MWT, while mediolateral local dynamic stability transiently declined during the first 60 s before stabilizing. This instability was associated with motor paralysis, suggesting trunk IMU-based sLE-ML may reveal motor control deficits not captured by walking distance or speed.

articles.title: Large language models for gait classification and treatment recommendation in cerebral palsy.
articles.authors: Meltem Çelik, Sema Ertan-Birsel, Elif Demirci et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Large language model (LLM)-based artificial intelligence systems are increasingly being explored for the interpretation of clinical and biomechanical data. However, their ability to classify cerebral palsy gait patterns and support treatment-related decision-making remains unclear. RESEARCH QUESTION: How accurately can commonly used LLM-based AI systems classify sagittal gait patterns in children with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy using kinematic graphs and three-dimensional skeletal gait videos, and how well do their treatment recommendations agree with expert decisions? METHODS: Fifteen children with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy, including three cases from each Rodda sagittal gait pattern, were retrospectively evaluated. ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude independently classified each case using bilateral sagittal-plane kinematic graphs and three-dimensional skeletal gait model videos and provided treatment recommendations. Expert consensus served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's and Fleiss' kappa, together with classification accuracy. RESULTS: Classification accuracy was higher in the graph-based condition than in the video-based condition. Claude showed the highest graph-based performance (73.3% accuracy; κ=0.67), while ChatGPT and Gemini each achieved 46.7% accuracy (κ=0.33). Video-based accuracy decreased to 26.7% for ChatGPT and Gemini (κ=0.08) and 20.0% for Claude (κ=0.00). Inter-model agreement was fair for graph-based classification (κ=0.31) but poor for video-based classification (κ=-0.07). Treatment recommendation agreement was generally low across models and modalities. SIGNIFICANCE: Under the tested conditions, LLMs achieved higher accuracy with kinematic graphs, although the difference cannot be attributed to input modality alone. Graph-based classification showed promising performance; however, limited treatment concordance indicates that current LLMs should be considered supportive rather than independent clinical decision-making tools.

articles.title: Conservation of a synaptic blueprint across the animal kingdom.
articles.authors: Aiden J Houcek, Ege T Kavalali
articles.abstract: Chemical synapses are fundamental computational units of the nervous system that enable rapid and precise information transfer through the nanoscale organization of presynaptic and postsynaptic components. Despite hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution and extraordinary diversity in nervous system architectures, the core physiological principles of chemical synaptic transmission remain remarkably conserved. Studies across Drosophila melanogaster, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, frogs and mammals reveal recurring principles governing active-zone organization, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, calcium signalling and postsynaptic specialization. Here, we examine the evolution of chemical synapses across the animal kingdom, focusing on the relationship between molecular diversification, nanoscale organization and functional conservation. We propose that the evolutionary stability of synapses reflects, in part, a stringent biophysical constraint imposed by the requirements for rapid chemical communication. We further consider how these conserved synaptic operations are assembled into neural circuits of dramatically different complexities, as well as the ctenophore nervous system as a critical test case for distinguishing molecular conservation from architectural and functional convergence. Across species, the emerging picture is that evolution has adhered to conserving the geometry and organizational principles of chemical synapses more stringently than a precise molecular composition. Synapses thus represent stable yet adaptable information-processing architectures in which conserved nanoscale constraints coexist with molecular flexibility and extensive diversification of neural circuits.
