articles.title: The gut-muscle-joint axis in osteoarthritis: Mechanistic insights and therapeutic perspectives.
articles.authors: Asima Karim, Firdos Ahmad, Rizwan Qaisar
articles.abstract: Emerging evidence highlights a complex crosstalk between the gut microbiota, musculoskeletal tissues, and the joint microenvironment, revealing osteoarthritis (OA) as a systemic disorder rather than a localized cartilage disease. The gut-muscle-joint interaction integrates microbial dysbiosis, chronic inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation to influence cartilage homeostasis, muscle strength, and neuromuscular stability. Building upon previously described gut-osteoarthritis and gut-muscle interactions, the Gut-Muscle-Joint (GMJ) axis is presented as an integrative framework linking intestinal permeability, microbial metabolites, systemic inflammatory signaling, neuromuscular health, skeletal muscle function, and joint integrity. Perturbations in this axis amplify oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and extracellular matrix degradation across musculoskeletal tissues. Understanding GMJ axis-driven mechanisms offers novel preventive and therapeutic strategies that target microbiome restoration, metabolic reprogramming, and neuromuscular health through probiotics, postbiotics, AMPK-SIRT1 activators, and structured exercise. This integrative perspective positions the GMJ axis as a unifying framework for intervention, enabling precision approaches to preserve joint function, reduce sarcopenia, and attenuate OA progression.

articles.title: Rethinking the application and adoption of NOVA classification in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs): a Southeast Asian food systems perspective.
articles.authors: C Jeyakumar Henry, M Aman Wirakartakusumah, E-Siong Tee et al.
articles.abstract: Ultra-processed foods have increasingly been associated with chronic disease risk in global analyses. The NOVA classification is positioned to influence dietary guidelines, food manufacturing, and public health policy worldwide. This paper argues that the NOVA classification, when applied without contextual adaptation, may be inappropriate for Southeast Asian food systems. It could misdirect policy interventions aimed at addressing both the double burden of under- and overnutrition. By labelling foods as UPFs, NOVA may obscure the essential role that certain processed foods play in improving nutritional outcomes and advancing public health. An overemphasis on the negative impact of processed and ultra-processed foods risks oversimplifying complex dietary patterns in Asia and other LMICs. It may also undermine nutritional gains achieved over the past four decades.

articles.title: Age and ethnicity influence serum holotranscobalamin ('Active' B12) and methylmalonic acid concentrations, two markers of vitamin B12 status assessment.
articles.authors: Agata Sobczyńska-Malefora, Maheen Siddiqui, Dominic J Harrington
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Serum vitamin B12 and holotranscobalamin (holoTC) are biomarkers of vitamin B12 status, often used with confirmatory tests such as methylmalonic acid (MMA). Serum B12 concentrations vary by age and ethnicity, but the impact of these factors on holoTC is unclear. METHODS: HoloTC was measured in 61,193 samples from an ethnically-diverse hospital population in London (Jan 2022-Oct 2023). HoloTC <25, 25-70 and >70 pmol/L were classified as deficient, indeterminate and replete, respectively. MMA was measured in 12,233 patients with holoTC 25-70 pmol/L. RESULTS: HoloTC concentrations differed significantly by ethnicity. Ethnic differences were minimal in children but became apparent in adulthood, with Black patients showing the highest holoTC concentrations, Asians intermediate, and White the lowest (p < 0.001). Overall, 1.7% of patients were holoTC deficient and 25.3% indeterminate. Among patients with holoTC 25-70 pmol/L, elevated MMA occurred in 32.7% of White, 14.8% of Black and 34.1% of Asian patients (p < 0.001) using age-specific MMA cut-offs ( > 280 nmol/L for ≤65 years; >360 nmol/L for >65 years). Using a higher MMA cut-off ( > 750 nmol/L), prevalence fell to 4.0%, 1.2%, and 4.7%, respectively. The overall prevalence of vitamin B12 deficiency in the entire cohort was 7.8% or 2.4%, depending on the MMA threshold. Compared with White patients, Black patients were 34.6% less likely to have elevated MMA. CONCLUSIONS: HoloTC and MMA concentrations vary significantly by age and ethnicity. Black adults exhibited higher holoTC and lower MMA concentrations, suggesting better B12 status or differences in metabolism. Age- and ethnicity-specific reference ranges for holoTC and MMA should be considered.

articles.title: Fish intake and mortality in Japan, a high fish-consuming country: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of cohort studies.
articles.authors: Kaori Yokoi, Hyeon-Ki Kim, Ayaka Kato et al.
articles.abstract: Fish consumption has been linked to decreased mortality risk in several prospective studies. However, most existing evidence is based on multi-regional analyses, and the dose-response relationship in populations with high habitual fish intake remains insufficiently characterised. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies among Japanese adults to assess the associations between fish consumption and all-cause and cause-specific mortality and to investigate potential dose-response relationships in a high-fish-intake population. We systematically searched the MEDLINE and Ichushi-Web databases. Prospective cohort studies conducted in Japan that reported hazard ratios or relative risks for fish intake and mortality outcomes were included. The protocol was registered a priori in the PROSPERO database (CRD42025635066). Random-effects models were used to calculate pooled estimates by comparing the highest and lowest intake categories. Dose-response relationships were evaluated using generalised least-squares trend estimation and restricted cubic spline models. A total of 113 articles were assessed for eligibility, and 16 studies met the inclusion criteria, and nine were eligible for meta-analysis. Higher fish intake was linked to lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.89-0.98) and cardiovascular disease mortality (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.80-0.91), with low heterogeneity. According to the GRADE framework, the certainty of evidence was rated low. Visual inspection suggested that mortality risk reduced with increasing fish intake up to approximately 100 g/day, after which the decline slowed, implying a plateau effect at higher intake levels. Among Japanese adults, high fish consumption was associated with a lower risk of all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality. Further research is required to clarify the dose-response relationship in populations with high fish consumption.

articles.title: Effect of a health belief model-based nutrition education intervention on dietary diversity among adults on antiretroviral treatment in Ilu Abbabor Zone, Southwestern Ethiopia - ERRATUM.
articles.authors: Ebissa Negera Gemechu, Tefera Belachew Lemma, Kalkidan Hassen Abate

articles.title: An observational study of food-related emotional expectancies, diet quality and comfort eating in the UK adult population.
articles.authors: Jenna R Cummings, Zoé Colombet, Emma Boyland
articles.abstract: According to expectancy theory, people eat food that they expect will bring positive emotions. The present research aimed to identify food and non-alcoholic beverages UK adults most expected to bring positive emotions; test influences of high fat, salt and/or sugar (HFSS) and branding on expectancies; and investigate associations of expectancies with diet quality and comfort eating (i.e. eating induced by negative emotions). A representative sample of UK adults (n 1203; Mage = 47 years; 52 % women; 87 % white) viewed food and non-alcoholic beverage images and completed the Anticipated Effects of Food Scale-Brief, a food frequency questionnaire, and questions about comfort eating and sociodemographic background. We ranked means of positive expectancies, conducted multilevel modelling to test influences of HFSS and branding on expectancies and examined correlations among expectancies, diet quality and comfort eating. Participants more strongly expected eating branded HFSS (e.g. Cadbury Twirl chocolate) v. generic non-HFSS (e.g. prawn curry) would result in positive emotions [b = 0·10, se = 0·04, p = ·02, 95 % CI (0·02, 0·18)]. Greater positive expectancies for HFSS - branded and generic - were associated with worse diet quality, especially positive expectancies for ice cream sundaes, fizzy drinks and chocolate (rs = -0·14 to -0·19, ps < ·001). Greater positive expectancies for HFSS and negative expectancies for HFSS and non-HFSS were associated with more frequent comfort eating (rs = 0·08 to 0·30, ps < ·05). Targeting positive HFSS expectancies through food environment policy and behavioural programmes may be a promising strategy for improving diet quality and reducing comfort eating in the UK adult population. Adults who comfort eat may also benefit from challenging negative expectancies for all foods.

articles.title: Validation of the GERY Protein Intake Screening Test among community-dwelling oldest-olds in Finland.
articles.authors: Riikka T Niskanen, Aava Ranta, Heli Salmenius-Suominen et al.
articles.abstract: Protein intake is often suboptimal among older adults, which may lead to protein-energy malnutrition, sarcopenia and frailty. A need exists for a simple, efficient and feasible protein-specific dietary assessment tool. Thus, a novel protein screening test, adapted to the Finnish cultural context, was developed. The aim of this study was to validate a novel protein screening test against a 1-d food record among Finnish older adults. Data were collected as part of the Helsinki Aging Study. The sample (N 140) consisted of Finnish community-dwelling oldest-old individuals (age range 80-100 years) with sufficient cognitive ability for at-home dietary assessment. A 1-d food record and the protein screening test were completed on one habitual eating day. Validity was assessed using the food record as a reference, with suboptimal protein intake defined as <1·2 g/kg BW/d. A Bland-Altman plot and concordance correlation coefficient (0·87, 95 % CI: 0·83-0·91) demonstrated good agreement between the methods. Sensitivity (0·85, 95 % CI: 0·72-0·94), specificity (0·81, 95 % CI: 0·71-0·88), area under receiver operating characteristic curve (0·90, 95 % CI: 0·85-0·95) and positive likelihood ratio (4·40, 95 % CI: 2·86-6·77) indicated strong diagnostic performance of the protein screening test. An optimal cut-off for the screening test to identify suboptimal protein intake was assessed at <1·00 g/kg BW/d. The novel protein screening test has good concurrent validity with the food record in identifying Finnish community-dwelling oldest-olds with suboptimal protein intake. It shows diagnostic potential for identifying individuals with suboptimal intake and to engage in targeted intervention.

articles.title: Dietary Inflammatory Index and cardiorespiratory fitness among older adults living in the community: a cross-sectional analysis.
articles.authors: Bi-Xia Huang, Zi-Hui Huang, Si Chen et al.
articles.abstract: The optimal dietary recommendation for healthy ageing remains unclear. This study examined the association between the Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) in Chinese community-dwelling older adults. Data were drawn from the Guangzhou Nutrition and Health Study's 3rd and 4th follow-up visits (2017-2021). DII was calculated from a Seventy nine-item validated FFQ, and CRF was assessed on a cycle ergometer using a submaximal constant work rate protocol. VO2max was estimated via the Åstrand-Ryhming Nomogram with age correction, and relative intensity was expressed as percentage of predicted maximal heart rate (%HRmax). Favourable CRF was defined as sex-specific VO2max in the top quartile or %HRmax < 85 %. Among 906 participants (615 women, 291 men; mean age 65·9 ± 5·4 years), those in the lowest DII tertile (anti-inflammatory diet) had higher VO2max than those in the highest tertile (P-trend = 0·048) and greater odds of favourable CRF (OR 1·81, 95 % CI 1·22-2·70), while no significant associations were observed for %HRmax (P-trend = 0·356; OR 1·31, 95 % CI 0·94-1·84). Associations between lower DII and higher VO2max were stronger among physically active participants (P-interaction = 0·049). Compared with consistently high DII, both transition to a low-inflammatory diet (OR 3·01, 95 % CI 1·20-7·51) and persistent adherence to such a diet (OR 2·49, 95 % CI 1·28-4·87) were associated with favourable CRF. These findings suggest that an anti-inflammatory diet is associated with better CRF in older adults, with potential synergistic benefits from physical activity.Trial registration: This trial was registered at clinicaltrials.gov as NCT03179657.

articles.title: Comparative digestive function and starch digestion kinetics in broilers and pigs.
articles.authors: Lucas Schmidt Bassi, Aaron J Cowieson, Sebastian Kaczmarek et al.
articles.abstract: This study compared starch digestion dynamics in broilers and pigs. Seven replicates of two broilers (24-d-old) and one pig (50-d-old) each were fed the same maize-based pelleted diet for 10 d, containing both solid (TiO2) and liquid (Cr-EDTA) markers. After 5 h of fasting, animals had 1 h of feed access before being euthanised at 2, 4, 6 and 8 h post-feeding. Digesta was collected from all pre-caecal segments. Jejunum and ileum combined were cut into four equal parts (SI1-4). Broilers had a heavier anterior tract and longer small intestine (SI) relative to live weight (P < 0·05), lower gizzard pH than the pig stomach (P < 0·05) and higher digesta DM. Duodenal digesta of broilers had a greater volume of particles <0·2 mm than pigs (P < 0·05). Apparent starch digestibility was higher in SI1-SI3 of broilers (P < 0·05), indicating more rapid starch digestion than pigs, although both species achieved similar digestibility (about 0·98) in SI4. Marker passage was unaffected by marker type but differed between species. Pigs showed higher proportion of markers exiting the anterior tract at 8 h (P < 0·05) and tended (P < 0·1) to have greater passage out of the SI, suggesting a more continuous flow pattern than broilers. Interval-based analysis showed similar marker passage out of the SI during 0-2 h, after which broilers had a pulsatile pattern, with reduced passage from 2 to 4 h, increased passage from 4 to 6 h and again lower passage from 6to 8 h (P < 0·05). In conclusion, broilers and pigs can attain comparable starch digestibility but rely on different kinetics and physiological mechanisms.

articles.title: Effect of Energy Restriction Combined with Probiotic Supplementation on Body Weight and Adiposity-Related Parameters in Adults with Overweight or Obesity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
articles.authors: Marcus V L Dos Santos Quaresma, Camila Guazzelli Marques, Ana Carolina Oumatu Magalhães et al.
articles.abstract: CONTEXT: Gut microbiota modulation has been proposed as an adjunct strategy for obesity management, but the additional effects of probiotics during energy restriction (ER) remain uncertain. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether probiotic supplementation combined with ER improves body weight and adiposity-related outcomes in adults with overweight or obesity compared with ER alone. DATA SOURCES: This systematic review and meta-analysis followed the PRISMA guidelines and was prospectively registered in PROSPERO. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and LILACS were searched through August 2025 for randomized controlled trials comparing ER plus probiotics with ER alone or ER plus placebo. DATA EXTRACTION: Two reviewers independently screened the studies and extracted the data. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence using GRADE. The primary outcome was body weight (BW); secondary outcomes were Body Mass Index (BMI), fat mass (FM), body fat percentage (BF%), waist circumference (WC), and fat-free mass (FFM). DATA ANALYSIS: Nineteen randomized controlled trials involving 1343 participants were included, of which 16 contributed to the meta-analysis. Interventions lasted 3-20 weeks, probiotic doses ranged from 1.8 × 106 to 1.5 × 1011 colony-forming units / day, and ER ranged from fixed deficits of 300-1000 kcal/day to relative reductions of 20% to 30%. Random-effects models showed no additional effect of probiotics on BW (mean difference [MD], -0.41 kg; 95% CI, -1.21 to 0.40), BMI (-0.12 kg/m²; -0.39 to 0.15), BF% (-0.63%; -1.52 to 0.26), WC (-0.33 cm; -1.06 to 0.39), or FFM (0.03 kg; -0.18 to 0.24). A small reduction in FM favored ER plus probiotics (-0.34 kg; -0.60 to -0.08; P = .016) and remained significant after excluding high-risk-of-bias studies. CONCLUSION: Adding probiotics to ER does not meaningfully enhance weight loss or body composition outcomes. Although FM was modestly reduced, the magnitude of the reduction was small, and its clinical relevance remains uncertain across the included randomized clinical trials overall. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration No. CRD42024619326.

articles.title: Menu Evaluation Tools in Food Services: An Integrative Review.
articles.authors: Lívia Bacharini Lima, Emanuele Batistela Dos Santos, Raquel Braz Assunção Botelho et al.
articles.abstract: CONTEXT: The growing demand for meals outside the home has boosted the food service sector, but there are constant concerns regarding the nutritional quality of the meals offered. In this scenario, menus play a strategic role in promoting health and in defining population dietary patterns. OBJECTIVE: This integrative review aimed to identify the instruments used to evaluate menus in food service settings across different contexts and target audiences. DATA SOURCES: This is an integrative review with a systematic search in the LILACS, Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science databases, with controlled and uncontrolled descriptors. Original studies published between 2003 and 2025 that described the development of menu evaluation instruments aimed at healthy food service were included. DATA EXTRACTION: Data were extracted on the characteristics of the instruments, including target population, food service setting, scope, evaluation approach, assessment perspectives, number of items, country of development, and validation status. DATA ANALYSIS: Data were summarized using descriptive statistics, including absolute and relative frequencies. A total of 29 studies were included, with a predominance of instruments aimed at children's menus (55.2%) and with a qualitative approach (72.4%). Brazil had the largest number of developed instruments, followed by Spain, the United States, and Portugal. Only 58.6% of the instruments presented some type of validation. The instruments varied in scope (menu or menu + context), evaluation method (qualitative, quantitative, or qualitative-quantitative), and the number of perspectives covered, with 10.3% multidimensional (ie, having 4 or more dimensions). CONCLUSION: The review showed advances in evaluating menus for the child population and in incorporating sustainability as an analytical parameter. However, gaps remain in validation and the development of multidimensional instruments, underscoring the need for validated and adapted tools to promote healthier, more sustainable menus.

articles.title: Dietary Polysaccharides for Overweight and Obesity Management: Targeting AMPK via the Gut Microbiota and Metabolites-A Review.
articles.authors: Zhongxing Chu, Zuomin Hu, Baitong Zhu et al.
articles.abstract: Obesity arises from dietary energy intake-expenditure imbalance. 5'-Adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a core regulator of biological energy metabolism, is a key target for obesity research and can be activated by endogenous stimuli, such as cellular stress and physical exercise. As natural active components with diverse sources and biological functions, dietary polysaccharides have shown potential lipid-lowering and antiobesity effects in preclinical studies. This narrative review systematically summarizes their structural characteristics, sources, absorption-utilization mechanisms and structure-activity relationships, focusing on their regulatory effects on obesity via the AMPK pathway. We searched PubMed and Web of Science for publications (2014-2026) using "dietary polysaccharides,""AMPK,""obesity," and "gut microbiota" as key words, screening original studies and reviews relevant to the core topic. Correlative evidence suggests that dietary polysaccharides are associated with altered expression of lipid metabolism-related factors through potential modulation of gut microbiota and its metabolites, with indirect links to AMPK activation. Such AMPK regulatory effects have tissue/organ specificity, and the causal relationship of each link remains to be rigorously established. Notably, the majority of current evidence derives from in vitro and rodent models, and extrapolation to human obesity management requires caution, as high-quality human clinical trials are urgently needed to validate the translational potential of these preclinical findings. This review clarifies the potential mechanism and existing research gaps of dietary polysaccharides in obesity alleviation, providing a scientific basis for the research and development of lipid-lowering functional foods based on dietary polysaccharides.

articles.title: An Empirical Snapshot of Local Nutrition Governance Capacity in the Rasuwa District of Nepal Before the Flood Surge of August 2026.
articles.authors: Patrick Webb, Robin Shrestha, Shibani Ghosh
articles.abstract: On August 26, 2026, flash floods swept through the Rasuwa district of Nepal, causing mass casualties and severe destruction. Research on disasters has led to valuable recommendations on how governments can be more attentive to warning signs and react more rapidly, and how tapping into local capacity and know-how can lead to more effective responses. However, in most crises not much is known about individual or institutional capacities that predated a shock or what resources donors and governments subsequently should bolster to support emergency responses and build resilience. In this Commentary, we draw on the self-reported data of civil servants and other local professionals tasked with implementing the national multisectoral nutrition strategy in Rasuwa. Data collection in 2024 predated the flood by roughly 2 years. The survey measured routine governance capacity, not disaster-response capacity specifically, and yet such data offer some insights into local capacity before the latest disaster and help our understanding of which elements were already under strain. The aim of this Commentary is not to report full survey findings but to highlight observations most relevant to the 2026 Rasuwa flood. Broadly, we suggest that routine governance research on nutrition and other technical topics of relevance can serve as a baseline for disaster recovery and that global calls for the localization of aid require much deeper understanding and measurement of local capacity to act.

articles.title: A Supplement Dose Is Not a Nutrient Requirement: When the Same Units Answer Different Questions.
articles.authors: Takuya Omura
articles.abstract: Clinical nutrition guidelines often contain numbers that look directly comparable but answer different questions. A supplement dose, a therapeutic total-intake target, and a population reference intake can all be expressed in grams of the same nutrient, yet they do not represent the same quantity. The risk is not that one number is wrong; it is that the wrong inference is drawn from a number that is right. Using the Nutritional Management Guidelines for Sarcopenia and Frailty 2025 as a current illustration, this commentary distinguishes 3 inferential layers: an implementation regimen, a therapeutic nutrition target, and a dietary reference value. The guideline suggests approximately 20-25 g/day of high-quality protein supplementation with exercise when intake is insufficient, while acknowledging that a recommended total daily protein intake for older people with sarcopenia or frailty cannot yet be specified. These statements are compatible, not contradictory. Moving from a tested regimen to a therapeutic total-intake target requires additional evidence on baseline intake, amount consumed, achieved exposure, comparator exposure, co-interventions, modifiers, and safety. Moving further to a dietary reference value requires a broader evidentiary scope focused on usual intake, intake-response relationships, safety, and population applicability. Guidance should therefore state what each number represents and what additional evidence is required before that number is transferred to a different inferential layer.
